H1.text: A ceiling fan blade. The second hand of a clock. A giant wheel at the fair.

H2.text: Each one goes round and round at a steady speed. So is anything really changing?

H3.text: Diya switches on the kitchen mixer. A drop of batter rides round the jar.

H4.text: Its speed never changes. So is the drop speeding up? Is it accelerating at all?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will see why the answer is yes.

P1.text: So what is uniform circular motion?

P2.text: An object moves along a circle, at a constant speed. Uniform means the speed stays the same.

P4.text: Every turn takes the same time. This time is called the time period, capital T.

S1.text: Let's run one in our motion notebook. A ball goes round a two metre circle, once every four seconds.

S2.text: Watch the speed in the readout. It stays at three point one four metres per second, all the way round.

S3.text: Now watch the blue velocity arrow. It always touches the circle, at right angles to the radius.

S4.text: Its length stays the same. But its direction keeps turning.

S5.text: The graph shows the two parts of the velocity. They rise and fall, while the speed stays flat.

S6.text: Let's slow it down and compare two moments.

S7.text: Here is the velocity now, and here it is a little later. Slide them tail to tail.

S8.text: The arrow that joins them is the change in velocity. It is not zero, and it points toward the centre.

D1.text: Now, how fast does the ball go? One step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. In one turn, the ball covers the whole circle. That distance is the circumference, two pi r.

D3.text: Step two. One turn takes one time period, T. So the speed v equals two pi r divided by T.

D4.text: Step three. Frequency, nu, is the number of turns in each second. So nu equals one over T.

D5.text: Step four. Put them together. v equals two pi r nu. Metres times turns per second gives metres per second.

D6.text: For our ball, that is pi. About three point one four metres per second.

T1.text: Remember this. In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant, but the velocity is not.

C1.text: Let's compare two kinds of steady motion, side by side.

C2.text: A ball rolls straight at three metres per second. Its arrow never changes. No acceleration.

C3.text: Another ball circles at three metres per second. Its arrow keeps turning. So there is an acceleration.

C4.text: Now you try. A car takes a curve at a steady sixty kilometres per hour. Is it accelerating? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Yes! Its speed is steady, but its direction is changing. A change in velocity is an acceleration.

R1.text: But which way does this acceleration point? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. The velocity always points along the tangent.

R3.text: Two. As the ball moves on, the arrow turns a little, always toward the centre.

R4.text: Three. So the change in velocity points toward the centre.

R5.text: Four. Acceleration points the same way as that change. So it points to the centre. We call it centripetal, meaning centre seeking.

K1.text: One more. A ball whirls on a string, and the string snaps. Which way does the ball fly? Pause and think.

K2.text: Along the tangent! At that moment its velocity points along the tangent, and nothing pulls it toward the centre any more.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. Back to Diya's mixer.

W2.text: A drop sits six centimetres from the centre. The jar makes twenty turns in two seconds. Find nu, T and the speed.

W3.text: Twenty turns in two seconds is ten turns each second. So nu is ten hertz.

W4.text: T is one over nu. That is zero point one second.

W5.text: v equals two pi r over T. That is two pi times zero point zero six, over zero point one.

W6.text: That is about three point seven seven metres per second. A steady speed, but the direction turns ten times every second.

X2.text: Many students write: the speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero.

X3.text: But in a circle, the direction keeps changing. So the velocity changes, and the acceleration is not zero. It points to the centre.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As short concept questions: what stays constant, what changes, and speed from the period.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A particle moves on a circle at a steady five metres per second, and turns through one hundred and twenty degrees. Find the change in speed, and the size of the change in velocity. Pause and solve.

A2.text: The speed is still five, so the change in speed is zero.

A3.text: Put the two velocity arrows tail to tail. The angle between them is one hundred and twenty degrees.

A4.text: So the change is the root of twenty five, plus twenty five, minus fifty cos one twenty. That is root seventy five, about eight point seven metres per second.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is a body in uniform circular motion accelerating, even at a steady speed?

Y3.text: Two. A string snaps while a ball goes round. Which way does the ball fly?

Y4.text: Three. How do you find the speed from the radius and the time period?
